:::{#exm-collision-entropy-three-values}
#### Collision entropy and entropy of a three-valued random variable

<!-- no-figure: the example is three numbers -->

Let $X$ take three values with probabilities $1/2$, $1/4$ and $1/4$.
The code below computes the expected [probability](https://morrison-lab.github.io/pds/probability-basics.html#def-probability),
the [collision entropy](#def-renyi-entropy) and the [entropy](https://morrison-lab.github.io/pds/expectation.html#def-entropy),
with base-2 [logarithms](https://morrison-lab.github.io/mds/algebra-exponentials.html#def-logarithm).

```{r}
#| label: collision-entropy-three-values
p <- c(1 / 2, 1 / 4, 1 / 4)
expected_prob <- sum(p^2)
collision_entropy <- -log2(expected_prob)
shannon_entropy <- -sum(p * log2(p))
c(
  expected_prob = expected_prob,
  collision_entropy = collision_entropy,
  shannon_entropy = shannon_entropy
)
```

By @thm-expected-probability-collision, the expected probability $\E{\P(X)} = `r expected_prob`$ is the [collision probability](#def-collision-probability).
The collision entropy is $H_2(X) = `r round(collision_entropy, 3)`$ [bits](#def-bit).
The entropy is $\entropyf{X} = `r shannon_entropy`$ bits.
As @thm-collision-entropy-at-most-entropy states, $H_2(X) \le \entropyf{X}$,
and the two differ because the three values are not equally likely.

:::
